analysis.one_liner: Raises the contract size below which federal construction projects can skip paying local prevailing wages.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in May 2017, sent to committee, and never received a vote before the 115th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal law requires contractors on federally funded construction to pay workers the locally prevailing wage — union-scale pay common to the area. This bill would raise the contract value where that requirement kicks in from $2,000 to $1 million, so most federally funded construction jobs would no longer have to pay the prevailing wage. It never left the House committee it was assigned to.
analysis.who_benefits: Construction contractors and firms bidding on federally funded projects. With the threshold at $1 million, most contracts could pay whatever wage the market allows — often less than the local prevailing rate — lowering labor costs on government work.

how_it_helps.text: Under the Davis-Bacon Act, federal construction, alteration, and repair contracts above $2,000 must pay laborers and mechanics the locally prevailing wage rate.
The bill would change that threshold from $2,000 to $1,000,000, so contracts below $1 million would no longer be required to pay prevailing wages.
The practical effect is that most federally financed construction projects would be exempt from the prevailing wage requirement, since few contracts reach $1 million.

analysis.who_pays: Construction workers on federally funded projects, who would earn whatever contractors offer instead of the area's prevailing wage. On many public building and highway projects that would mean a cut in hourly pay.

drawbacks.text: Workers on exempted contracts could be paid less than the local standard for their trade, since the prevailing wage floor would no longer apply to most federal construction.

Proponents of prevailing wage rules argue the standards prevent low-bid contractors from undercutting local pay scales on public projects; the bill would remove that protection for contracts under $1 million.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would lower labor costs for contractors on federal projects, but those savings come directly out of construction workers' hourly pay on public jobs. It is a straightforward shift of cost from contractors to workers, with no offsetting protection for the affected workers.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Education and the Workforce Committee, which never took it up before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Jeff Duncan of South Carolina introduced the bill on May 25, 2017.
It was referred to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce.
The action history shows no further steps — no markup, no floor vote — and the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Construction workers keep prevailing-wage protection on federally funded projects. Contractors who would have gained a lower-wage exemption on most public work did not get it.

for.name: Rep. Jeff Duncan
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill raising the Davis-Bacon prevailing-wage threshold to $1 million.

for.name: 7 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it all-Republican sponsorship.

against.name: House Committee on Education and the Workforce
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for markup or a vote; it died in committee.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had only Republican sponsorship (one sponsor plus seven Republican cosponsors) and no floor vote ever occurred, so no partisan vote split was recorded.

industries.note: The bill would have let them pay below the local prevailing wage on any contract under $1 million, cutting labor costs on most public building work. The savings come out of workers' paychecks.
The Davis-Bacon prevailing wage floor is a pay standard for these workers; the bill would remove it from most federal projects, putting downward pressure on their hourly wages.
